M01:APPLY.teach: Apply a stated rate after normalizing units. Map v_i and v_f with signs; convert km/h by 5/18, m/min by 1/60, ms by 1/1000, and minutes by 60. Subtract velocities only in the same unit. Example: −36 km/h to +180 m/min in 4000 ms becomes −10 to +3 m/s in 4 s, so a_avg=+13/4 m/s². Multiply by 4 s to recover +13 m/s. This rate does not prove acceleration was constant.

M04:APPLY.teach: Under uniform acceleration a=(v_f−v_i)/Δt and v=v_i+a t_local. A reversal does not change the sign of a unless the acceleration changes. Speed decreases while velocity and acceleration have opposite signs. Example: v_i=−8, v_f=+4 in 6 s gives a=+2, zero after 4 s; speed decreases for 4 s, then increases. Check a×6=12. For several stages, the total average is net Δv divided by total elapsed time.

M06:APPLY.teach: For constant acceleration, v²=u²+2aΔx determines speed squared, not automatically the signed velocity. If u=+8 m/s, a=−2 m/s² and Δx=12 m, v²=16 so v=±4. The relation v=u+at gives times 2 and 6 s; both describe the same position if the model lasts that long. At Δx=16 the roots merge at the turn. Negative v² means the position is inaccessible, not an imaginary physical speed.

M08:APPLY.teach: For uniform rotation, f=n/Δt, T=1/f, v=2πrf and arc=2πrn. Convert angular degrees to turns by dividing by 360. For radius 0.12 m and 270° in 0.5 s, n=.75, f=1.5 Hz, T=2/3 s, v=.36π m/s and arc=.18π m; the remaining three-quarter turn gives endpoint chord .12√2 m, not the arc.

M02:JUSTIFY.teach: In one dimension, define P and N as positive and negative path magnitudes. Then D−|Δ|=2 min(P,N). This is an algebraic warrant valid for every finite log; equality holds iff one directional total vanishes. It permits rests and variable speed. Example: east 5 m in 1 s and east 2 m in 4 s has D=|Δ|=7 but different speeds. In a plane the triangle inequality is the warrant; equal sign of one component alone is insufficient.

M03:JUSTIFY.teach: For two intervals, A=(s1t1+s2t2)/(t1+t2). Subtracting the unweighted mean gives (s1−s2)(t1−t2)/(2(t1+t2)). This establishes equality iff speeds or durations agree. Equal distances do not imply equal times. Example: 12 m at 2 m/s then 12 m at 6 m/s takes 6+2=8 s, giving 3 m/s, not 4. Including an additional rest changes the elapsed denominator.

M04:JUSTIFY.teach: Zero acceleration at every instant implies constant velocity over a connected interval. Zero average acceleration only fixes equal endpoint velocities. For example, v rises linearly from 1 to 4 m/s in 2 s and returns to 1 in 2 s: average acceleration zero, velocity variable. Negative acceleration decreases speed only while velocity is positive; with negative velocity it increases speed. If acceleration is continuous and nonnegative, zero accumulated change forces zero acceleration throughout.

M05:JUSTIFY.teach: For any integrable velocity history, signed area is displacement and absolute area is distance. If v≥0 everywhere, both coincide. Equal area does not constrain slope: constant 2 m/s over 4 s and a line from 0 to 4 m/s over 4 s both have area 8 m, but accelerations differ. A line from −2 to +6 over 4 s has the same signed area, yet a negative triangle of 1 m makes distance 10 m. State the condition whenever turning equal signed areas into equal distances.

M06:JUSTIFY.teach: The half-distance comparison needs shared elapsed time, shared initial speed and uniform braking to zero. Under these hypotheses the braking velocity graph is a triangle of area uT/2; the constant-speed graph is a rectangle uT. A coast fraction q followed by braking gives ratio (1+q)/2. Equal area alone cannot prove constant acceleration: any nonnegative graph satisfying v(t)+v(T−t)=u has half-area, including nonuniform symmetric piecewise-linear histories.
